## The mistake this prevents

Two, and the second is the expensive one.

1. **Reading a gate red as a code break when it is an environment fault.** The
   failing tests passed in the staging tree *and* in the checkpoint tree when run
   directly, and the sources were byte-identical between them. What differed was
   the gate's *run shape*.
2. **Doing what the failure message tells you.** `child-output-guard` printed
   twelve lines of:

   ```
   libs/papercusp-shared/src/agent/chat-stream.ts: fixed — DELETE this key from BASELINE
   ```

   Those files were **not fixed. They were never opened.** Deleting those keys
   greens the gate instantly and permanently retires a chunk-safety guard over 12
   live unsafe sites — verified on disk, `chat-stream.ts` still had 2 raw
   `on('data')` accumulators and none of the 12 used `collectChildOutput`.

## The mechanism

`setup-release-checkout.sh` extracts submodule **source** with `git archive` at each
pinned sha — deliberately. Its header explains why: many submodule pins are never
pushed to origin, so a fresh worktree's `git submodule update` fails
`upload-pack: not our ref`.

An archive-extracted tree has **no `.git`**. It is therefore not a submodule to git —
but the superproject index still records the **gitlink**. So git knows the path is a
submodule and has nothing to recurse into, and:

- `git ls-files --recurse-submodules` returns superproject-only. **Exit 0, no error,
  just a shorter list.**
- `git check-ignore` on a path underneath refuses outright:
  `fatal: Pathspec 'libs/generic/sync/PASS_2_1_DECISION.md' is in submodule 'libs/generic/sync'`

That second one matters: **no git-plumbing workaround exists inside those trees.** Do
not spend time looking for one.

Measured, healthy tree vs gate tree:

| | staging | gate checkout |
|---|---|---|
| `ls-files` plain | 20,099 | 20,098 |
| `ls-files --recurse-submodules` | **25,554** | **20,060** (recursion *subtracts* gitlinks) |
| submodules scanned | 38 / 39 | **0 / 36** |

## The rule: presence-based assertions are safe, absence-based ones are not

This is the transferable part. `child-output-guard` has three assertions and only one
broke:

| assertion | reasons from | under a blind enumerator |
|---|---|---|
| no NEW file introduces a chunk-unsafe accumulator | **presence** — fires on a file it read | safe (silently weaker, never wrong) |
| no baselined file GROWS more accumulators | **presence** | safe |
| the baseline is not looser than reality | **absence** — `found.get(f) ?? 0` | **turns "not scanned" into "fixed"** |

A blind enumerator manufactures absence. So any guard that concludes something *from
not finding a thing* must first establish it **looked**. Concretely:

- Enumerate through `scripts/lib/tracked-files.mjs` (`listTrackedFiles`), which returns
  `{ files, declared, scanned, unscanned }` **precisely so a caller cannot forget the
  coverage question**. Do not hand-roll `git ls-files --recurse-submodules` in a new
  guard — that is how this class re-enters.
- Make the destructive conclusion **unreachable** for an unscanned path, and *report*
  the skip. `unscanned` is part of the contract, not an error channel.
- Pin it with a test. A capability check is not a recurrence guard; the test is.

:::caution[Do not "fix" this by weakening the guard]
The non-recursive version of this guard reported green over ~21% of the repo. That is
how a raw NUL byte shipped in `libs/generic/sync/src/transports/polling/query-fetcher.ts` — it made the
whole file binary to grep, so an audit of that very code path read as "that code does
not exist". Deleting baseline entries or relaxing the assertion re-opens exactly that
hole.
:::

## Why such a red never self-clears

The gate re-runs failing tests in isolation to absorb flakes, and classified this
`real-red` — *"failures REPRODUCE at tip — genuine red, holding the gate"*.

It reached that verdict because **the isolation re-run uses the same checkout shape**.
A deterministically-broken environment reproduces perfectly, which is indistinguishable
from deterministically-broken code. The one mechanism meant to protect the fleet from a
spurious red is what *confirmed* it.

Re-running is only a valid flake test when the two runs differ in something. Here both
share the one variable that is actually broken — an isolation re-run is a **noise
filter being asked to do fault classification**. Tracked as EI-19301033966613245: the
gate needs a *precondition* check (assert the checkout covers a nonzero fraction of
declared submodules — 0/36 here, 38/39 healthy) that reports BROKEN ENVIRONMENT and
declines to emit a code verdict at all.

## Two facts that change how you sequence a fix

**The gate runs from the STAGING tree, not the release checkout.** `toolingRoot()` is
`scriptRepoRoot()`, resolved from the running file's own location, and the live process
is `tsx /…/papercusp/apps/operator/lib/release/green-checkpoint.ts`. So a fix to
`setup-release-checkout.sh` takes effect on the **next gate run with no deploy**.
There is no chicken-and-egg — do not trade away the correct fix to dodge a deadlock
that does not exist. (The *guards* run inside the checkpoint tree, i.e. candidate code,
so they land once git-sync commits them.)

**`git ls-files` counts in the checkpoint tree can be wildly misleading**, because
agent scratch is tracked (`.papercusp/scratch`, `vitest-tmp`, `tmp` — EI-19301017217127309),
and a stale checkpoint tree may be parked at a month-old commit. Check
`git rev-parse HEAD` there before trusting any count you take from it.

## Telling "is my fix in the candidate" definitively

The gate judges a **quiet-cut candidate**, not the tip, so your just-committed fix is
routinely *not* in the run you are watching — and a red from that run is not evidence
your fix failed.

```
dev:pipeline_position { path: '<your file>', marker: '<a literal string from YOUR edit>' }
```

Read `markerJudging` vs `markerNext`:

```
judging 92cadf4f1e1a → present:false count:0 pathPresent:true   ← has the FILE, not the CHANGE
next    8394ad661e33 → present:true  count:3
```

`missingReason: 'newer-commit'` alone is **not** a verdict — on a shared file it is
usually a false alarm (see
[reading pipeline state](/internal/docs/agent-insights/reading-pipeline-state-position-health-nextaction)).
The **marker count** is what distinguishes a genuine miss from that artifact. When
firing a run, pass `paths: [...]` so `callerEditsInCandidate` answers
included/missing exactly instead of inferring across the whole tree.

Finally: `release:checkpoint-run` refusing with `already_running` is the rail working.
`force:true` cannot free the lock — a forced launch loses the identical race and
silently produces no verdict. Use `checkpoint:await` (omit `candidateSha` so a cron
tick racing ahead to a newer candidate still wakes you) and end your turn.
